transcript: 200 years ago there was a chess player so strong that he quit chess forever because nobody in the world could compete with him. [music] His name was Paul Morphy and this is a composition by him. White has a pawn and a rook against [music] the two pawns of black and this black bishop. But there's a problem. White cannot simply take this pawn with the rook because otherwise the black bishop is going to capture it back. And after we take the bishop, this game is actually going to be won by black. He's going to run with the black pawn to the other side of the board and get a new queen. If white simply waits with his rook [music] and goes for example here, hoping that the bishop leaves, black is actually going to push this pawn and now there is not going to be any way to make any progress in the position. And if the white rook moves anywhere else, white is simply going to take this last pawn. And after the white rook comes back to check the black king, now the bishop is going to be able to cover it like this. So white needs to realize that his best asset is not this powerful rook, but instead this little innocent pawn. In fact, the only winning move for white is the brilliant rook to A6. And now, if the bishop simply moves away, the pawn is going to be captured by the rook and this is going to be a beautiful checkmate. And some of you might think, "Well, Peter, this doesn't make sense. The rook can simply be captured by this black pawn." But if black does that, well, now this white pawn is going to get free access to the B7 square and with the help of his royal king, that is going to be checkmate.
